rounds.proof_sketch: eps changed from 1e-5 to 1e-4. When variance≈1.53e-7 (one outlier of 0.1 among 65536 zeros): inv_std_original≈316.23, inv_std_mutant=100. For outlier: normalized=0.1×inv_std, giving 31.6 vs 10, difference=21.6 >> tolerance 0.01+0.01×31.6≈0.33
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the epsilon value in LayerNorm from 1e-5 to 1e-4. Standard random inputs typically have moderate variance, which dominates the eps term, making the difference negligible. However, when variance is extremely small (near zero), eps becomes the dominant term in sqrt(variance + eps), causing a ~3.16x difference in the normalization factor. Carefully crafted low-variance inputs expose this behavioral difference.
rounds.kill_strategy: Create inputs with near-zero variance by setting most elements to the same value (0) and only one element per normalization window to a different value (0.1). This makes eps dominate the denominator, amplifying the difference between 1e-5 and 1e-4 into a ~3x scale factor.
rounds.recommendations: LayerNorm implementations should be tested with low-variance inputs (constant or near-constant values) to verify epsilon parameter sensitivity. Mutation tests on numerical stability parameters like eps should include adversarial low-variance test cases.
rounds.suggested_code:
def generate_inputs(device):
    # Shape: [16, 64, 256, 256] - creates very low variance per feature window
    x = torch.zeros(16, 64, 256, 256, dtype=torch.float32, device=device)
    # Set one element per normalization window to create tiny non-zero variance
    # This makes eps dominate the sqrt(variance + eps) computation
    x[:, :, 0, 0] = 0.1
    return [x]
